Abstract
Reservoir computing (RC) presents a computationally efficient alternative to
conventional recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for temporal-data processing.
Traditional bio-inspired auditory systems often face constraints due to limited
computational power and high energy consumption, which impede speech-
recognition accuracy. In this work, we demonstrate high-performance ferro-
electric neuromorphic devices based on TiN/WOx/Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO, 4 nm)/
TiN heterostructures for constructing an artificial auditory nervous system for
efficient voice recognition. The device exhibited a high remanent polarization
(Pr) of approximately 20.58 μC cm–2 at 1.8 V and endurance exceeding
1010 cycles. Density functional theory calculations and experiments confirm
that the WOx interlayer regulates oxygen vacancy formation and migration
within the HZO layer. By emulating essential biological synaptic plasticity
functions, such as paired-pulse facilitation and long-term potentiation/inhibi-
tion, the ferroelectric tunnel junction-based devices can perform signal
processing and neural computation within the RC framework, achieving an
accuracy beyond 99% across 12 categories of everyday vocabulary voice words.
These findings provide a promising pathway for developing highly reliable and
energy-efficient neuromorphic artificial auditory systems.

ture of the human auditory system to capture, process,
and identify sound precisely. Their development has
attracted attention, particularly in medical rehabilitation
and
bionic
robotics.1–3
However,

auditory systems that separate sensing, storage, and com-
putation are limited by computational power, energy con-
sumption, and integration density, hindering speech
recognition accuracy.4–7
Inspired by the brain's efficient, low-power informa-
tion processing, neuromorphic engineering promises to
address these bottlenecks.8–12 Recent progress in ferroelec-
tric neuromorphic devices has shown potential for energy-
efficient and high-performance computing applications,
including
exploring
various
2D
materials
and
heterostructures for memristor-based reservoir computing
(RC).13–17 Ferroelectric tunnel junction (FTJs) emulate
synaptic behavior, providing a promising avenue for devel-
oping neuromorphic devices. When composed of a ferro-
electric layer sandwiched between two electrodes, FTJs
exhibit tunable resistive states under external stimuli,
mimicking biological synapses' excitation and inhibition
processes. Precisely controlling their conductance changes
allows for high-fidelity emulation of synaptic weights,
enabling high-performance weight updates and learning
functions in artificial neural networks. Compared to tradi-
tional complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor devices,
the low operating voltage and current of FTJs reduce
energy consumption and boost system efficiency.18–20
However, attaining both stable high polarization and high
endurance continues to be a significant difficulty for
many FTJs.
RC, a potent machine learning paradigm for handling
intricate temporal data, has attracted significant atten-
tion. In RC systems, a dynamic nonlinear “reservoir”
maps time-varying inputs into a high-dimensional fea-
ture space, and a trainable readout performs linear
weighted summation, reducing computational costs rela-
tive to traditional recurrent neural networks (RNNs).21–23
The integration of ferroelectric devices into RC systems
has demonstrated promising results in various applica-
tions
such
as
speech
recognition
and
time-series
prediction.24–26 For instance, Li et al. developed an artifi-
cial visual recognition system based on a MoS2-HZO
memristor
array,
integrated
with
sensor-based
RC,
thereby achieving efficient time-series data processing at
reduced training costs.27 Similarly, Chen et al. have
reported
an
all-ferroelectric
RC
system
utilizing
Pt/BiFeO3/SrRuO3 ferroelectric diodes that achieved a
normalized root mean square error of 0.017 in time-series
prediction.28 Nonetheless, residual polarization, endur-
ance, and switching speed still limit the performance of
ferroelectric devices. Furthermore, the application of RC
for speech recognition remains relatively under-explored
compared to other domains like image recognition.
In this work, we successfully constructed a high-
performance neuromorphic hearing system by controlling
the intercalation thickness to engineer oxygen vacancy
concentration in FTJ devices. Incorporating a WOx
interlayer into the TiN/WOx (1.5 nm)/HZO (4 nm)/TiN
device structure delivers a Pr of 20.58 μC cm–2 at 1.8 V
and endurance exceeding 1010 cycles. Density func-
tional
theory
(DFT)
calculations,
corroborated
by
experimental results, confirm that the WOx interlayer
modulates oxygen vacancy dynamics within the HZO
layer. Within a RC framework, the resulting artificial
auditory system has demonstrated excellent speech rec-
ognition capabilities, achieving a classification accu-
racy of up to 99% for 12 common spoken words. This
work highlights ferroelectric neuromorphic devices as
candidates for energy-efficient, high-performance, self-
powered artificial auditory systems.

Ferroelectric tunnel junction
device based on HZO
Figure 1A illustrates the RC architecture for artificial voice
recognition, in which input data are nonlinearly mapped
into a high-dimensional feature space. This mapping pro-
cess captures temporal dynamics, analogous to the short-
term memory of biological synapses, thereby achieving
efficient
voice
recognition
and
classification.29–31
Figure 1B shows the device structure—a Si substrate, a
TiN layer, a HZO layer, a WOx layer, and a top electrode.
The
cross-sectional
transmission
electron
microscopy
(TEM) image in Figure 1C further reveals a well-defined

Figure 1D displays grazing incidence x-ray diffraction

(1.5 nm)/HZO/TiN device exhibits the highest proportion
of the ferroelectric o-phase, thus indicating enhanced fer-
roelectric performance. Additionally, x-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) analysis (Figure 1E) verifies WOx
intercalation.

2.2

Excellent ferroelectric properties of
the device, including high residual
polarization and endurance
We evaluated how WOₓ interlayer thickness affects
device performance and, by extension, RC behavior.
Before wake-up cycling, all devices exhibited clear
antiferroelectric behavior (Figure 2A). After 106 wake-up
cycles under a 1-kHz square wave pulse with an ampli-
tude of 2.4 V, the WOx-1.5 nm device delivered the
highest Pr of 20.58 μC cm–2 at 1.8 V, outperforming both
the WOx-0 nm (15.01 μC cm–2) and WOx-3 nm (10.73 μC
cm–2) devices (Figure 2B). The optimal 1.5 nm WOx
interlayer likely acts as an effective oxygen scavenger,
thereby reducing oxygen vacancies and stabilizing the
ferroelectric o-phase. A thicker interlayer may weaken
the electric field distribution across the HZO layer, thus
decreasing the ferroelectric polarization.
Meanwhile, since the insertion of WOx may affect
the electric field applied to HZO, the Pr versus normal-
ized electric field intensity for devices with different
WOx thicknesses was calculated to confirm further the
superiority of the WOx-1.5 nm device (see Figure S2).
Figure 2C compares the endurance characteristics of
the WOx-0, WOx-1.5, and WOx-3 nm devices under
cyclic experiments with a triangular pulse of ±1.8 V
and a pulse frequency of 100 kHz. The WOx-0 nm
device suffered significant polarization fatigue after
107 cycles, likely due to cumulative Joule heat and
charge trapping effects caused by considerable leakage
current. After 2  109 cycles, the WOx-0 nm device had
already broken down. In contrast, the WOx-1.5 nm
device maintained a stable Pr of 3 μC cm–2 after
1010 cycles. These results indicate that the insertion of
a WOx dielectric layer is beneficial for improving the
endurance of TiN/HZO/TiN devices. Retention tests
also

for

memory

S3).
Figure 2D,E presents the coercive field evolution and
the I–V curves, respectively. The WOx-1.5 nm device
maintained a stable coercive field of 1 MV cm–1 at
1.8 V, while the WOx-0 nm device exhibited an increas-

2.3
|
Oxygen vacancy engineer's device
performance
XPS analysis was conducted to unveil the mechanism
responsible for the enhanced ferroelectric performance of
the WOx-1.5 nm device. As shown in Figure 3A–C, the
WOx-1.5 nm device exhibits a significant reduction in oxy-
gen vacancy concentration compared to the WOx-0 nm
device. The ratio of oxygen vacancies to lattice oxygen
(vacancy peak intensity at 532 eV to lattice oxygen peak)
was determined to be 39.11% for WOx-0 nm, 25.36% for
WOx-1.5 nm, and 30.31% for WOx-3 nm, respectively. An
optimal oxygen vacancy concentration stabilizes the o-
phase and enhances polarization characteristics, whereas
excessive oxygen vacancies cause fatigue effects and hard
breakdown, severely affecting the life of the device.39–42
These vacancies accumulate at interfaces, potentially pin
domain walls, and reduce the switchable polarization. The
bond dissociation energy of W-O (476.4 kJ mol–1) is signifi-
cantly lower than that of Hf-O (801 kJ/mol) and Zr-O
(766 kJ mol–1), indicating that WOx dissociates more read-
ily, thus releasing oxygen to fill the excess oxygen vacan-
cies in HZO, enhancing ferroelectricity and endurance.
The XPS results further reveal the presence of distinctive
peaks corresponding to W5+ in the 4f orbitals of W at the
WOx-1.5 and WOx-3 nm interfaces (Figures 3D and S5),
which exert precise control over the oxygen content at the
WOx-HZO interface, thus constituting a pivotal factor in
the
augmentation
of
device
performance.43
Electron
energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) analysis revealed that the
ratio of the a/b peak intensity decreases with the increas-
ing oxygen vacancy concentration. As shown in Figure 3E,
the a/b intensity ratio of the O K edge near WOx was
determined to be 0.918, significantly higher than that near
HZO (0.906). This aligns with the hypothesis of lower
vacancy concentration at the WOx interface. Finally, the
DFT simulation (Figure 3F) shows a significantly lower
formation energy for oxygen vacancies at the interface
when compared to the HZO bulk, thus facilitating oxygen
diffusion and vacancy filling. Detailed calculation proce-
dures are provided in the Supporting Information.

2.5
|
Device-based speech recognition RC
system
The FTJ device shows strong sub-threshold nonlinear I–V
behavior and short-term memory, exactly the non-linear
mapping and temporal storage required by RC. Current
is highly sensitive to pulse width and amplitude, so small
input variations can produce distinct states. Meanwhile,
the natural decay of the EPSC provides a short-term
memory window that forms the basis for time-dependent
dynamic processing.
Figure 5A shows that we implemented an RC voice-
recognition
pipeline.
The
FTJ
device
acts
as
the
nonlinear
reservoir,
transforming
time-series
audio
inputs into high-dimensional states. The dataset of Chi-
nese daily expressions was constructed using wearable
speech sensing devices, consisting of audio recordings of
12 daily expressions spoken by four males and three
females, each with a sampling rate of 16 kHz, a bit
depth of 16 bits (Figure S14), and an audio duration of
2 s (Table S1). Subsequently, mel-frequency cepstral
coefficients (MFCC) transformed the raw audio into
20-dimensional spectral features. A discrete cosine
transform was applied to select the most significant
12 dimensions. The channel values of each spectrum
were transmitted for training over a duration τ. Within
each time window τ, the 12-dimensional MFCC feature
vector was multiplied by a random mask matrix of
binary values (1 and 1), generating a voltage sequence
normalized to 2.5 to 2.5 V. The device's current
response, representing the reservoir state, was sampled
at a fixed time interval δ; these samples constituted the
reservoir state. The number of virtual nodes generated by
a single device is M ¼ τ=δ, and the total number of virtual
nodes is N M, where N is the number of devices. The
linear output layer outputs a 12-dimensional one-hot
encoded vector as the recognition result. We split the
dataset (804 samples) into a 3 : 1 ratio and trained the
read-out with ridge regression to avoid over-fitting. By
comparing the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embed-
ding
(t-SNE)
plots
of
the
original
MFCC
features
(Figure 5B) and the output of the RC system (Figure 5C),
the effectiveness of the model in separating different cate-
gories can be verified. In Figure 5B, the original features
overlap severely in the t-SNE plot, indicating difficult
direct classification. The RC and subsequent classifica-
tion layers in Figure 5C separate previously overlapping,
proving that the system has successfully extracted dis-
criminatory features (Figure S17). As illustrated in
Figure 5D, the relationship between the node count and
recognition accuracy was investigated by increasing the
mask length to augment the number of virtual nodes
(more details are presented in Figure S18). The area
under the curve (AUC) values shown in Figure 5E, which
captures the classifier's overall discriminative power, con-
firm the model's reliability. When 100 reservoir nodes
were used, the model achieved an accuracy of around
88% in Figure 5D but an AUC exceeding 95% in
Figure 5E. This indicates that even though some samples
were misclassified at the chosen threshold, the classifier's
ranking ability remained strong across the full range of
thresholds. When the number of reservoir nodes was
increased to 1000, the AUC values for all categories
surpassed 99%, consistent with the observed accuracy
improvement to approximately 98%. These results con-
firm that enlarging the reservoir increases the pointwise

CONCLUSION
TiN/WOx(t nm)/HZO/TiN
ferroelectric
neuromorphic
devices have been successfully fabricated, demonstrating
a high remanent polarization (Pr) of approximately 20.58
μC cm–2 at 1.8 V and an endurance exceeding 1010 cycles
following activation. DFT calculations, XPS, and EELS
analyses confirm that the WOx interlayer effectively
reduces
oxygen
vacancies
within
the
HZO
layer.
Neuromorphic devices exhibit tunable conductance states
under external stimulation, thereby enabling them to
mimic biological synaptic functions, such as synaptic
plasticity. Integrated into an RC framework, these devices
achieve an accuracy of over 99% in classifying 12 types of
everyday speech commands. These results highlight fer-
roelectric neuromorphic devices as energy-efficient, high-
performance RC building blocks, paving the way for
future advancements in artificial intelligence. Future
hardware translation will require three engineering
thrusts:
transferring
the
stack
onto
flexible,
skin-
conformal substrates to meet the mechanical demands of
wearable electronics; scaling the architecture into dense
crossbar arrays with sub-100-nm pitch while mitigating
sneak-path
interference;
and
implementing
a
full
backend-of-line, low-temperature packaging scheme that
endures aggressive thermal cycling without degrading
device performance. These directions frame our ongoing
efforts to translate the demonstrated device-level merits
into robust, manufacturable systems for next-generation
wearable and Internet of Things applications.

EXPERIMENTS
TiN/WOx/HZO/TiN ferroelectric synaptic devices were
fabricated on a 2-inch p-type silicon (p-Si) wafer. A
40-nm-thick TiN bottom electrode was deposited on the
SiO2/Si substrate using physical vapor deposition in an
Ar/N2 atmosphere. Subsequently, 4-nm-thick Hf0.5Zr0.5O2
(HZO) ferroelectric thin films were deposited by atomic
layer deposition at 280C using TEMAHf, TEMAZr, and
H2O as precursors (Figure S1). A 4-nm HZO layer pro-
vides the optimal trade-off for our WOx-inserted FTJ: thin
enough for efficient tunneling and sub-2V switching, yet
thick enough to suppress leakage and maintain high rem-
anent polarization and endurance. The WOx layer was
then deposited by sputtering at a power of 120W and a
pressure of 0.5 Pa to modulate oxygen vacancies in the
HZO layer. Electrode patterns were defined using photo-
lithography, followed by the deposition of a 40-nm-thick
TiN top electrode. After device fabrication, rapid thermal
annealing (RTA) at 550C for 30 s in a N2 atmosphere
was
performed
to
optimize
device
performance.
High-purity nitrogen (99.9%, residual O2 < 3 ppm) is
used throughout the process; after an initial 60 s purge,
the nitrogen flow is held at 2000 sccm during the isother-
mal soak. The temperature is ramped up at 20C min–1,
maintained for the prescribed dwell time, and then
cooled at 10C min–1 under the same 99.9% N2 flow. XRD
phi scan analyses were performed with the Bruker D8
DISCOVER. The P–V loops and endurance were mea-
sured with a ferroelectric workstation (Radiant Precision
Multiferro II). The electrical performance tests were car-
ried out with Agilent B1500A and KEITHLEY 4200.

Abstract: Reservoir computing (RC) presents a computationally efficient alternative to conventional recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for temporal-data processing. Traditional bio-inspired auditory systems often face constraints due to limited computational power and high energy consumption, which impede speech- recognition accuracy. In this work, we demonstrate high-performance ferro- electric neuromorphic devices based on TiN/WOx/Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO, 4 nm)/ TiN heterostructures for constructing an artificial auditory nervous system for efficient voice recognition. The device exhibited a high remanent polarization (Pr) of approximately 20.58 μC cm–2 at 1.8 V and endurance exceeding 1010 cycles. Density functional theory calculations and experiments confirm that the WOx interlayer regulates oxygen vacancy formation and migration within the HZO layer. By emulating essential biological synaptic plasticity functions, such as paired-pulse facilitation and long-term potentiation/inhibi- tion, the ferroelectric tunnel junction-based devices can perform signal processing and neural computation within the RC framework, achieving an accuracy beyond 99% across 12 categories of everyday vocabulary voice words. These findings provide a promising pathway for developing highly reliable and energy-efficient neuromorphic artificial auditory systems.
